message.content: When Nicolaus Copernicus founded his heliocentric theory in the early sixteenth century, Europe was still anchored in Ptolemaic astronomy and medieval cosmology. Politically, the Holy Roman Empire remained a patchwork of principalities, while papal authority, Reformation disputes, and Ottoman pressure reshaped intellectual loyalty and patronage. In Poland, royal courts and the church offered relative stability, yet scholars still faced censorship, ecclesiastical scrutiny, and the need to frame radical ideas cautiously. The intellectual climate was not cactiform, but dense with competing theological, legal, and astronomical expectations.
